title: Hamburger Steak
subtitle: A thick beef mince patty with onion gravy, no bun
excerpt: A thick, well-seasoned beef mince patty cooked in a cast iron skillet and served with a rich onion gravy. Old-fashioned American diner food at its most satisfying.
sourceNotes: Classic American diner hamburger steak with onion gravy, drawing from Southern US and mid-century diner cooking traditions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked patties and gravy separately. Defrost overnight and reheat gently in a covered pan.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily. Shape the patties ahead and keep refrigerated until cooking.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shape and season the patties up to 24 hours in advance. Store covered in the fridge.

content.text: Hamburger steak is a thick beef patty served on a plate, not in a bun. Use beef mince with a decent fat content for the best crust. Press a small dimple in the centre of each patty so they cook flat rather than puffing up.
Combine the beef mince with the garlic powder, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix briefly. Divide into 4 equal patties about 2cm thick. Press a small dent in the centre of each with your thumb.

Heat the oil in the cast iron skillet over a high heat until smoking. Cook the patties for 3 to 4 minutes without moving them. Flip once and cook for a further 3 minutes. Remove and rest for 3 minutes.
In the same skillet, reduce the heat to medium. Add the butter and onions. Cook for 10 minutes until the onions are soft and starting to colour, stirring often.
Sprinkle the flour over the onions and stir for 1 minute. Gradually pour in the beef stock, scraping up any browned bits from the base of the pan.
Add the Worcestershire sauce. Simmer for 4 minutes until the gravy thickens. Taste and season.
Return the patties to the pan and warm in the gravy for 1 minute. Serve with the onion gravy spooned over.

items.symptom: The patties puff up in the middle during cooking.
items.cause: No dimple was pressed in the centre before cooking.
items.fix: Always press a thumb dent in the centre of each patty before it hits the pan. This keeps them flat.

items.cause: The pan was not hot enough or the patties were moved before the crust formed.
items.fix: Get the pan smoking hot before the patties go in. Leave them completely alone for the first 3 minutes.

items.symptom: The gravy has lumps in it.
items.cause: The stock was added too quickly to the flour.
items.fix: Add the stock in a slow stream while stirring constantly. A whisk works better than a spoon here.
